habit_line: Focus habit: Notice - Pause on the picture or the numbers and let the child say what they see before you name anything. Say: “What do you see? What stays the same, what changes?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Welcome, Area Architects! Architects must know two things about every room: how much floor it covers, and how far it is all the way round.
Today we find areas and perimeters of tricky shapes WITHOUT counting every square, and we test a big idea: does the same area always give the same perimeter? Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
do: Focus habit: Notice - Pause on the picture or the numbers and let the child say what they see before you name anything. Say: “What do you see? What stays the same, what changes?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: I will read out a job. If the job needs the space INSIDE, hold up A for area. If it goes ROUND THE EDGE, hold up P for perimeter.
Be ready to explain: "It covers the floor, so it is area." "It goes round the outside, so it is perimeter."
You have 12 square tiles. How many different rectangles do you think you can make with all 12? Will they all have the same perimeter? Write your guess in the corner of your whiteboard.
stuck: Stuck: start with one long row of 12. Then try 2 rows. Then 3 rows.
Not sure if a rectangle is new: "Is it the same as one you have, just turned round?"
Finished early: try 16 tiles. Which rectangle has the smallest perimeter now?

say: “An L-shape. I need every side. The bottom is 8 cm and the top part is 5 cm, so the step across must be 8 − 5 = 3 cm. The left is 6 cm and the right is 4 cm, so the step down is 6 − 4 = 2 cm.”

“For the area I can split it into a 5 by 6 rectangle and a 3 by 4 rectangle: 30 + 12 = 42. Or I can draw the big 8 by 6 rectangle and take away the missing 3 by 2 piece: 48 − 6 = 42. Same answer, so I trust it.”

“For the perimeter, I push the two step sides out. The 3 cm piece slides up to the top and the 2 cm piece slides across to the right. Now it is an 8 by 6 rectangle, so the perimeter is 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 cm.”

do: Ask: “Which side is opposite this one? How can that help you find the missing length?”
Ask: “Can you find the area another way to check?”
Ask: “You cut the shape and moved a piece. What stayed the same? What changed?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Mark every side with its length before you start. Use the opposite sides.”
Hint 2: “Draw the big rectangle round the shape. What is missing?”
Hint 3: “Push the steps out. Does the outline become a rectangle?”

say: “Ben says a bigger area always means a bigger perimeter. Can you find two rectangles that prove him wrong?”
ask: “Ben says a bigger area always means a bigger perimeter. Can you find two rectangles that prove him wrong?”
Ben is wrong. A 1 cm by 12 cm rectangle has area 12 cm² and perimeter 26 cm, but a 4 cm by 4 cm square has a bigger area (16 cm²) and a smaller perimeter (16 cm).

say: “Today you were real architects: you split shapes, took pieces away and pushed steps out instead of counting every square.”
“Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p4l7-title.note: Objective: Find the area of a composite figure by splitting it into rectangles or by taking away a missing piece, find its perimeter by pushing the steps out to a rectangle, find every rectangle with a given area and compare their perimeters, and explain what changes when a shape is cut and rearranged. Thinking strategies taught today: SPLIT IT or TAKE AWAY, PUSH THE STEPS OUT, and MAKE A LIST IN ORDER. Materials: 1 cm square tiles or 24 paper squares per child, 1 cm grid paper, scissors, a 30 cm ruler, mini whiteboards, a paper strip 8 squares by 2 squares for cutting. Online: children cut out paper squares and 1 cm grid strips before the lesson and build on camera; the tutor draws on the grid figures on the slides. Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 3-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6.5 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 8.5 to 11.5 (three questions). Explore 11.5 to 23.5 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 23.5 to 29 (click to reveal each step and answer; there is no "your turn" slide today). Brain break 29 to 32.5 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 32.5 to 78.5: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 32.5 to 48.5, check together 48.5 to 50.5, short teaching before page 2 50.5 to 54, page 2 on your own 54 to 75 (the last 3 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 75 to 78.5. Talk time 78.5 to 83.5 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout; one minute is the tool question: where did you use today's tool?). Exit ticket 83.5 to 87.5. Looking back 87.5 to 90 (common look-back: 90-second timer, then about 60 seconds to stamp journals). Pairs: Q1 and Q2. Then Q3 alone. After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children). SPINE: Today's tool is Spot the pattern. Look for what repeats or changes by the same amount, then say the rule. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Notice. Pause on the picture or the numbers and let the child say what they see before you name anything. Say: "What do you see? What stays the same, what changes?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p4l7-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6.5 (5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) 14 squares (the full 5 by 3 rectangle is 15 squares, and 1 is cut out). 2) The same: 16 units for both. Push the cut-out corner back out. The two edges of the notch are just as long as the two edges of the corner they replace. A GOOD REASON: For area, count the squares or take away the piece that is missing. For perimeter, push the corner back out to a rectangle. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "Pairs: Q1 and Q2. Then Q3 alone. After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l7-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Area or Perimeter? Children make two cards (or write A and P on two halves of a whiteboard). Read each job aloud. Count 3, 2, 1 and everyone shows A or P. Then click to reveal (clicks go job 1 to job 6). Listen for "it covers the floor" (area, square units like m²) and "it goes round the edge" (perimeter, units like m). Job 5 is the one to argue about: the wood goes round the photo, so it is perimeter; the glass in the frame would be area. Quick finisher if there is time: a job where you need BOTH (a garden: grass seed for the area, a fence for the perimeter). Watch for children who say "area is length times breadth" without knowing what it measures: ask them to point to the area on the slide.

p4l7-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 11.5. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. Three questions, about 30 seconds each. Insist on units: cm for perimeter, cm² for area. No follow-up questions. For 3: 48 ÷ 8, or which number times 8 makes 48. Answers: 42 cm², 36 cm, 6 cm. The other two warm-up questions (perimeter of a 12 by 5 rectangle; a square with perimeter 28 cm, its area) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l7-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 20.5. Pairs build rectangles with 12 tiles (online: paper squares on camera, or draw on 1 cm grid paper). Ask them to predict first: "How many rectangles? Will they all have the same perimeter?" Many children think the same tiles must give the same perimeter. Let them find out. Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: try 16 tiles. Which rectangle has the smallest perimeter now? (4 by 4, 16 cm.) GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): What if you use 24 tiles? Make every rectangle. Which has the smallest perimeter? Answer: 4 rectangles: 1 × 24 (perimeter 50 cm), 2 × 12 (28 cm), 3 × 8 (22 cm) and 4 × 6 (20 cm). The 4 by 6 has the smallest perimeter: it is the closest to a square.

p4l7-explore2.note: Minutes 20.5 to 23.5. Pencils down (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms), then gather the rectangles on the board in the order children say them. Two debrief questions only. Then ask "Is any missing? Is any the same as another, just turned?" Answers: 1) 3 rectangles: 1 by 12, 2 by 6, 3 by 4 (12 by 1 is the same as 1 by 12 turned). 2) 1 by 12 has 26 cm; 3 by 4 has 14 cm (2 by 6 has 16 cm). The third question (all have the same area, so why are the perimeters different?) is not asked. The area is the number of tiles, which never changes; the perimeter counts the outside edges, and close to a square hides the most edges. Do NOT give the rule yet if nobody says it: the teaching part comes back to it.

p4l7-teach1.note: Teach. Ask first: "Can we find the area yet?" (No: we do not know every length.) Click 1: run a finger along the bottom (8 cm) and then along the top: 5 cm plus the step across. Think-aloud: "The bottom goes all the way across. The top and the step across together go the same distance. 8 − 5 = 3." Click 2: the same going down: 6 = 4 + the step, so 2 cm. Click 3: the general idea. Check by counting grid squares: 3 and 2.

p4l7-we1.note: Click 1: colour the two rectangles: "I split the shape with one line. Left part 5 by 6, right part 3 by 4. I need the lengths of EACH part: the right part is 8 − 5 = 3 wide and 4 tall." Click 2: "Or I draw the big rectangle round the whole shape: 8 by 6 = 48. The piece that is missing is 3 by 2 = 6. 48 − 6 = 42." Click 3: both agree. Ask: "Could we split it a different way?" (Yes: across, into 5 by 2 on top and 8 by 4 underneath: 10 + 32 = 42.)

p4l7-we2.note: Ask first: "We know all six sides now. How do we find the perimeter?" Add them going round, starting at the top left corner: 5 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 8 + 6 = 28. Then: "Is there a quicker way?" Click 1: slide the step sides with your finger. Think-aloud: "The 3 cm side is level with the top, so if I slide it up it fills the gap in the top edge: 5 + 3 = 8. The 2 cm side slides right to sit on top of the 4 cm side: 2 + 4 = 6." Click 2: the dashed rectangle. Click 3: same answer. Click 4: the warning, which comes back before page 2. Note: the AREA did change (48 versus 42); only the outline length is the same.

p4l7-key.note: Say the key ideas together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Adding only the labelled sides of an L-shape, or giving a missing side the wrong length instead of using the opposite sides. (2) Thinking the same area means the same perimeter, or that cutting a corner off makes the perimeter smaller. (3) Finding the area of a border as 2 × (length + breadth) and forgetting the 4 corner squares.

p4l7-break.note: 3.5 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 32.5): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. Call out "long and thin", "square", "long and thin" faster and faster. Then: "Everyone stand up tall and stretch: is your area or your perimeter changing?" (Neither is a real rectangle, it is just for fun.)

p4l7-ws1.note: Minutes 32.5 to 48.5. Pairs do Q1 and Q2. Split Q1 between the partners: partner A splits the figure into two rectangles, partner B uses the big rectangle minus the missing piece, then they compare (about 4 minutes, not 6). Q3 (six tiles) is the first question each child does on their own, at the start of page 2 time; its answer is checked with page 2. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "Pairs: Q1 and Q2. Then Q3 alone. After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l7-ws1ans.note: Click after a pair explains. Q1b: split into 4 by 7 and 5 by 4, or 9 by 7 take away 5 by 3. Q1c: push out: 9 + 7 + 9 + 7 = 32. Q2: the rectangle closest to a square has the smallest perimeter. (The 36 cm² question, 6 by 6 with perimeter 24 cm, is in the question bank.)

p4l7-teachstair.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 is a staircase with different numbers). Ask first: "Can we find the perimeter when the steps have no labels?" Click 1: trace the three red sides and push them up with your finger: "however long each step is, together they reach all the way across, 8 cm." Click 2: the same for the green sides: "together they go all the way down, 5 cm." Click 3: the rectangle. Then check by counting the grid: 2 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 8 + 5 = 26. Remind them of the warning from before: a gap in the middle of a side adds extra.

p4l7-teachcut.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 cuts a different rectangle). Use a real paper strip and scissors. Click 1: area and perimeter of the strip (6 × 2 = 12; 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16). Click 2: cut and stack. Click 3: the area. Click 4: the perimeter. Click 5: the big idea. Ask: "Why did the perimeter go DOWN?" (The two halves now share a long side inside, so 3 cm of edge on each piece is hidden. The new shape is closer to a square.)

p4l7-teachframe.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6 is a photo frame with different numbers). Click 1: "The path is on BOTH ends, so the length grows by 1 + 1." Many children add only 1. Click 2: big take away small. Click 3: the check, with the corner squares lit up: "If I only count the four strips beside the garden, I miss the corners."

p4l7-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who still think cutting a corner off makes the perimeter smaller. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Do question 3 first, then Q4 and Q5. Q6 is a choice for the end. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 3 minutes of this block (minute 72 to 75) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l7-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3 (six tiles, done first on their own): each pair of tiles that share a side hides 2 cm of edge. 6 tiles have 24 cm of edge; a row hides 5 × 2 = 10, leaving 14; the 2 by 3 hides 7 × 2 = 14, leaving 10. Q4a: the across sides add up to the bottom (11 cm) and the down sides add up to the left (6 cm). Counting: 3 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 11 + 6 = 34. Q5: stack the two 4 by 2 halves. Q6c: Mei counted only the strips beside the photo.

p4l7-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) 1 by 30 (62 cm), 2 by 15 (34 cm), 3 by 10 (26 cm), 5 by 6 (22 cm). Smallest: 5 cm by 6 cm, 22 cm. 2) 1 by 9 (9 cm²), 2 by 8 (16 cm²), 3 by 7 (21 cm²), 4 by 6 (24 cm²), 5 by 5 (25 cm²). Largest: the 5 cm by 5 cm square, 25 cm². 3) Area 96 − 4 × 9 = 60 cm². Perimeter 40 cm, the same as the rectangle: each cut takes away 3 + 3 and adds 3 + 3. 4) Area 4 + 9 + 16 = 29 cm². Perimeter 26 cm: push the steps out to a 9 cm by 4 cm rectangle.

p4l7-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q6 and Q7. Answers: 1) 63 m² (slide the paths to the edges: the grass is 9 m by 7 m). 2) 6 cm (the area is 36 cm² and 6 × 6 = 36); the perimeter went down from 26 cm to 24 cm.

p4l7-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: Q1 "Would the grass area change if the paths were moved?" Q2 "What stays the same when we cut and move pieces? So what is the area of the square?" Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l7-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: sliding pieces without overlapping keeps the area, the same idea as Q5. The check needs care: 10 + 8 = 18 counts the 1 m square where the paths cross twice. Q2: if anyone wants to see the cut, it is a staircase: from the top at 3 cm, down 2 cm, across 3 cm, down to the bottom. Slide the right piece 3 cm left and 2 cm up and it makes the 6 cm square. Draw it on 1 cm grid paper to check.

p4l7-talk.note: Minutes 78.5 to 83.5. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then share. Answer: Ben is wrong. A 1 cm by 12 cm rectangle has area 12 cm² and perimeter 26 cm; a 4 cm by 4 cm square has a bigger area (16 cm²) but a smaller perimeter (16 cm). One counter-example is enough to show a rule is not always true. Not asked in class (moved to the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math): "When we cut a shape and move the pieces, which stays the same?" (The area, because nothing is added or lost; the perimeter can change.) Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake. TOOL MINUTE: Talk time is one minute longer than before (the common look-back is shorter). Spend it on the question on the slide: where did you use today's tool, and what did it help you see? Listen for the tool named, not for the answer; a child may pass.

p4l7-exit.note: Minutes 83.5 to 87.5. Answer: area 35 − 4 = 31 cm²; perimeter 24 cm, the same as the 7 by 5 rectangle (push the corner back out). Children who write 20 cm for the perimeter forgot the two new sides; children who write 31 cm mixed up area and perimeter. Extension: Ravi has 24 m of fencing for a rectangular pen with whole-metre sides. One side is a wall and needs no fence. What is the largest area? (72 m²: 6 m, 12 m, 6 m.)

p4l7-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 87.5 to 90. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. HABIT: Focus habit: Notice. Pause on the picture or the numbers and let the child say what they see before you name anything. Say: "What do you see? What stays the same, what changes?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
